g6-2023-037.lessonTitle: Formula for the Area of a Triangle
g6-2023-037.quote: For each triangle, identify a base and a corresponding height
g6-2023-037.why: The item shows a right triangle with both legs labelled (22 ft and 25 ft) and asks for its area - one clean application of A = 1/2 b h where the two given lengths are already a base-height pair. This Cool-down is where the curriculum tests exactly that: it hands students labelled triangles and asks them to pick a base and its corresponding height and use them to find the area. Lesson 9 Activity 1 'Finding a Formula for the Area of a Triangle' (p160) is where the formula is generated; the Cool-down is where it is assessed.

g6-2024-028.quote: find the area of quadrilaterals that are not parallelograms
g6-2024-028.why: The item gives an isosceles trapezoid with both parallel sides (10 cm, 16 cm) and the height (15 cm) and asks for its area. Lesson 11 Activity 2 is the one place in grade 6 that asks students to find the area of a quadrilateral that is not a parallelogram, by decomposing it into triangles and rectangles. Its 'Are You Ready for More?' extension is literally 'write a formula for the area of a trapezoid', and Lesson 11 practice problem 3 (p201) is 'Find the area of this trapezoid.'

g6-2024-040.quote: What is the area of the shaded part of the flag?
g6-2024-040.why: The item shows a rectangular flag 9 cm by 5 cm with a triangular notch cut out of it and asks for the area of the shaded section - a whole-minus-triangle subtraction. This Cool-down asks the same question in the same context, word for word: a flag with a shaded part, find that area, explain your reasoning. Lesson 11 Activity 2 'Quadrilateral Strategies' (p191) is the later, more general runner-up, but nothing else in the course matches this item's context and question as exactly.

g6-2025-017.quote: students determine the area of an unfamiliar polygon
g6-2025-017.why: The item gives a regular hexagon built from six equilateral triangles, with a side of 5 cm and a centre-to-side height of 4.3 cm, and asks for the hexagon's area - decompose the polygon into triangles, use the triangle formula, multiply by six. The Pinwheel activity is the only activity in grade 6 that asks for the area of a polygon with more than four sides by decomposing it into triangles; it is optional. The non-optional runner-up in the same lesson is Activity 2 'Quadrilateral Strategies' (p191), which asks the same kind of decomposition but only for quadrilaterals. Lesson 11 practice problem 4 (p202) is this exact item - 'Lin decomposed the hexagon into six identical, equilateral triangles' for a regular hexagon - but it is a practice problem, not an activity.

g6-2025-036.quote: decompose the quadrilateral into parallelograms and triangles to find the area
g6-2025-036.why: A dashed vertical height divides a parallelogram into an unshaded triangle and a shaded trapezoid; the item asks for the shaded area (parallelogram 2.4 by 3 = 7.2, minus a triangle 1.2 by 3 halved = 1.8, giving 5.4). Activity 2 is where students are asked to plan and choose among exactly these moves - decompose into parallelograms and triangles, or enclose and subtract - to find the area of a quadrilateral that is not a parallelogram. Lesson 3 Activity 2 'Off the Grid' (p65) asks 'Find the area of the shaded region(s) of each figure', but it comes before the parallelogram base-height work this item needs.

g6-2026-029.lessonTitle: Formula for the Area of a Triangle
g6-2026-029.activity: Applying the Formula for Area of Triangles
g6-2026-029.quote: Each diagram is labeled with two or three measurements
g6-2026-029.why: A parallelogram of sailcloth is split by a diagonal into two triangles and one is shaded; the figure labels the top (8 m), the height (6 m) and the slanted side (10 m), so the student must ignore the 10 and compute 1/2 times 8 times 6 = 24. That choosing-among-labelled-measurements move is exactly what this activity sets up: students first circle a base measurement they can use, then find the area, with each diagram carrying two or three measurements. Lesson 8 Warm-up 'Composing Parallelograms' (p141) supplies the other half of the reasoning - a triangle is half of the parallelogram with the same base and height.

g6-2026-043.quote: enclose the figure in a rectangle and subtract the area of the extra pieces
g6-2026-043.why: The item gives a right trapezoid with parallel sides 11.5 cm and 15.2 cm and a distance of 8.8 cm between them, and asks for its area; NYSED's own exemplary response splits it into a rectangle (11.5 by 8.8) and a triangle (3.7 by 8.8 halved). Activity 2 is the activity that asks students to find the area of a non-parallelogram quadrilateral by exactly these strategies, and Lesson 11 practice problem 3 (p201) is 'Find the area of this trapezoid. Explain or show your strategy.'

g6-2023-033.quote: What is the volume, in cubic inches, of the rectangular prism?
g6-2023-033.unitBasis: NY-6.G.2 is tabled in both Unit 1 and Unit 4. Unit 1 Section D reaches volume only through whole unit cubes and the distinction between surface area and volume; the fractional-edge-length work this item needs - packing a prism with 1/2-, 1/3- and 1/4-inch cubes and then multiplying the edge lengths directly - happens in Unit 4 Section D, so the unit comes from the item.
g6-2023-033.why: A labelled diagram of a right rectangular prism, 8 in by 1 3/4 in by 5/8 in; multiply the three edge lengths to get 8 3/4 cubic inches. This activity hands students a prism with a fractional edge length (3 in by 1 in by 1 1/3 in) and asks for its volume in cubic inches, establishing that the product of the edge lengths is the volume even when the edges are fractions.

g6-2023-045.quote: the volume of rectangular prisms given the area of the base
g6-2023-045.unitBasis: NY-6.G.2 is tabled in both Unit 1 and Unit 4. Unit 1 Section D reaches volume only through whole unit cubes and the distinction between surface area and volume; the fractional-edge-length work this item needs - packing a prism with 1/2-, 1/3- and 1/4-inch cubes and then multiplying the edge lengths directly - happens in Unit 4 Section D, so the unit comes from the item.
g6-2023-045.why: This item is the odd one out among the volume questions: it gives the area of the base (42 sq ft) and the height (5 3/4 ft) rather than three edge lengths, so the student must know V = base area times height. The Fish Tank activity is described as solving word problems that find the volume of rectangular prisms given the area of the base and its height - the only activity in the unit framed that way - but it is optional. The non-optional runner-up is the Lesson 15 Cool-down 'Storage Box' (p238), which gives a base ('3 inches by 4 inches') and a fractional height, but as two base dimensions rather than an area.

Unit 1 Lesson 17 'Squares and Cubes' covers cubes but only with whole-number edges.

g6-2024-035.unitBasis: NY-6.G.2 is tabled in both Unit 1 and Unit 4. g6-2024-035.why: A cereal box described in words as 8 1/10 in by 4 4/5 in by 12 1/2 in; the answer, 486 cubic inches, comes from multiplying the three mixed numbers. The Cool-down is the same task on a real box with a fractional dimension: find the volume in cubic inches and show the reasoning.

g6-2025-034.why: A gift box 7 3/5 cm by 5 4/5 cm by 2 1/2 cm; multiply the three mixed numbers for 110 1/5 cubic centimetres. Like the item, the Cool-down describes a real box in words, gives its dimensions with a fraction among them, and asks for the volume.

g6-2025-043.quote: Find the length of the tray in inches. Show your reasoning.

The Lesson 13 Cool-down 'Two Frames' (p214) assesses the mirror image of it (given area and length, find the width) and is a close second.

g6-2026-011.quote: The box can be packed with 144 cubes with an edge length of 1/2 inch.

g6-2026-035.quote: students continue the work on finding the volume of a right rectangular prism

g6-2023-007.activity: Using Nets to Find Surface Area
g6-2023-007.quote: Find the surface area of each polyhedron. Explain your reasoning clearly.
g6-2023-007.why: The item shows the net of a right square pyramid (8-inch square base, triangular faces 10 inches tall) and asks for the surface area: 64 + 4 times 40 = 224 square inches. Lesson 14's narrative says students 'assemble two prisms and a pyramid from given nets and use nets to find the surface area of each polyhedron', and its learning target is 'When given a net of a prism or a pyramid, I can calculate its surface area' - the item's task exactly. Lesson 15's summary works a square pyramid (square base plus four triangles) and is the runner-up.

g6-2024-032.activity: Surface Area of a Triangular Prism
g6-2024-032.quote: In this net, the two triangles are right triangles.
g6-2024-032.why: A skateboard ramp is a right triangular prism, given as a net (6 by 4 ft rectangle, triangles of height 2.5 ft, slanted faces 6.5 ft); surface area 75 square feet. This Cool-down is the same task in the same words: a net whose two triangles are right triangles and whose quadrilaterals are rectangles, find its surface area and say which polyhedron it makes.

g6-2025-013.quote: Find the surface area (in square units) of the polyhedron.
g6-2025-013.why: The item gives the net of a right rectangular prism (2 cm by 2 cm faces, 5 cm long) and asks for the surface area, 48 square centimetres. This Cool-down is precisely that two-part question - identify the polyhedron the net makes, then find its surface area - and it is where the skill is assessed rather than introduced.

g6-2025-042.activity: Using Nets to Find Surface Area
g6-2025-042.quote: students cut and assemble nets into polyhedra. They use nets to find surface area
g6-2025-042.why: The net of a right square pyramid with a 5 cm base and 3.5 cm triangle heights; 25 + 35 = 60 square centimetres, shown work required. Same task as g6-2023-007: given a net of a pyramid, find its surface area, which is this activity's stated work and Lesson 14's learning target. The activity also asks students to organise their work so others can follow it, which matches the constructed-response demand.

g6-2026-016.activity: Surface Area of a Triangular Prism
g6-2026-016.quote: What is its surface area in square units? Show your reasoning.
g6-2026-016.why: The net of a right triangular prism - three rectangles 10, 12 and 10 feet wide and 6 feet tall, with a triangle of base 12 and height 8 above and below the middle rectangle - surface area 288 square feet. Same task as this Cool-down, with one difference worth noting: the Cool-down's two triangles are right triangles, while this item's are isosceles, so the student must read the triangle's height off the figure rather than use a leg.

g6-2023-042.lessonTitle: Using Diagrams to Find the Number of Groups
g6-2023-042.quote: How many groups of 1/2 pound are in 2 3/4 pounds?
g6-2023-042.why: A box holds 8 1/4 cups of cereal and a serving is 3/4 cup: how many servings? That is the 'how many groups of this size are in that amount' interpretation of division, with a mixed-number total and a fractional group size. This activity asks exactly that, in context, and asks students to write the multiplication or division equation and explain their reasoning - which is what the 2-credit item wants shown.

g6-2024-015.lessonTitle: Using Diagrams to Find the Number of Groups
g6-2024-015.quote: students apply the reasoning strategies they learned in earlier activities to solve division problems
g6-2024-015.why: 1 1/4 pounds of nuts into 1/8-pound bags: how many bags? The activity's first question is the same sentence with different numbers - how many groups of a fractional pound are in a mixed number of pounds. Lesson 10 Activity 1 'Dividing by Unit Fractions' (p163) is the runner-up: it is where dividing by a unit fraction is generalised to multiplying by its denominator, which is the shortcut this item's distractors (5/32, 1 1/8, 2) are built to punish.

g6-2025-006.lessonTitle: Using Diagrams to Find the Number of Groups
g6-2025-006.why: A 4 1/2 cup carton and a 3/4 cup serving: how many full servings? The Cool-down asks the same question with the same divisor - how many 3/4 s are in a given amount - and asks for the equation and a tape diagram. It is the assessment point for the 'how many groups?' interpretation with a non-unit fractional divisor.

g6-2026-009.lessonTitle: Dividing by Unit and Non-Unit Fractions
g6-2026-009.quote: find how many halves, thirds, fourths, or sixths were in 6 wholes
g6-2026-009.why: 2 1/2 cakes at 1/12 of a cake per serving gives 30 servings. With a divisor of 1/12 a diagram is impractical, so the item depends on the generalisation this activity builds: to divide by a unit fraction 1/b, multiply by b. The activity's closing prompt is to find how many halves, thirds, fourths or sixths are in a whole number 'without counting all the parts', which is the reasoning the item requires.

g6-2026-046.quote: how many whole batches of ornaments can they make?
g6-2026-046.why: 4 3/4 cups of bananas at 1/3 cup per full batch gives 14 1/4, and the answer is 14 - the item's whole demand is that a part batch does not count. This activity is the only place in grade 6 that asks for the whole number of batches that can be made from available ingredients, and it even uses 1/3 cup per batch in a recipe context. Lesson 16 is an optional lesson. The non-optional runner-up is Lesson 6 Activity 2 'Finding the Number of Groups' (p95), which asks the same division but never asks students to discard the remainder.

g6-2024-044.quote: A cube has edge length 5 in. Use an exponent to express its volume.
g6-2024-044.unitBasis: NY-6.G.5 is absent from the guide's standard-to-lesson table in all three grades and has no statement in data/standards.json, so the unit comes from the items alone. Both items show a cube built from unit cubes and ask which perfect cube its volume represents, one of them asking for exponents in the explanation. Unit 1 Section E 'Squares and Cubes' is the only place in grade 6 that defines a perfect cube, ties it to the volume of a cube built from unit cubes, and introduces the exponent 3 for it.
g6-2024-044.why: A prism 4 unit cubes along each edge; the answer is 64, which is 4 cubed, and the item explicitly asks the student to 'include what you know about volume and exponents'. This activity is the only one that asks students to express the volume of a cube using an exponent, in exactly that geometric context. Activity 2 'Perfect Cubes' (p291) supplies the other half - the term 'perfect cube' and the volume of a 4 cm cube - and Activity 1 'Building with 32 Cubes (Optional)' (p289) is the unit-cube model the item pictures, but it is optional.

g6-2026-022.quote: students think about examples and non-examples of perfect cubes
g6-2026-022.unitBasis: NY-6.G.5 is absent from the guide's standard-to-lesson table in all three grades and has no statement in data/standards.json, so the unit comes from the items alone. Both items show a cube built from unit cubes and ask which perfect cube its volume represents, one of them asking for exponents in the explanation. Unit 1 Section E 'Squares and Cubes' is the only place in grade 6 that defines a perfect cube, ties it to the volume of a cube built from unit cubes, and introduces the exponent 3 for it.
g6-2026-022.why: A model of 5 layers of 5 rows of 5 unit cubes; which perfect cube does it represent? 125. This activity is where students meet the term 'perfect cube', decide which numbers are and are not perfect cubes, and find the volume of a cube from its edge length - the item's whole task, and unlike g6-2024-044 it does not ask for exponent notation. Activity 1 'Building with 32 Cubes (Optional)' (p289) builds the same unit-cube model but is optional.

g6-2025-033.unitBasis: NY-5.OA.3 is a grade 5 standard on a grade 6 paper; there is no grade 5 curriculum in this repository, so the project's home-grade rule has no grade to search, and grade 6 was searched instead.
g6-2025-033.why: The item gives two recursive rules (x increases by 3, y increases by 2) and a starting point (1,1), asks the student to generate the ordered pairs, and then to pick the graph that shows them. A keyword sweep of every activity in all nine grade 6 units found nothing that asks students to generate ordered pairs from rules of that kind. Grade 6 does teach the plotting half - Unit 7 Lesson 11 'Points in the Coordinate Plane' Activity 1 'The Coordinate Plane' (p142) has students plot and label ordered pairs, and Unit 6 Lesson 18 (optional) has them graph ordered pairs taken from a table - but no activity asks for the pairs to be generated from a pair of 'each value is n more than the one before it' rules, and that generation is where this item's work and its distractors live. Stretching a coordinate-plane lesson to cover it would misrepresent what the curriculum asks.

g6-2026-042.unitBasis: NY-5.OA.3 is a grade 5 standard on a grade 6 paper; there is no grade 5 curriculum in this repository, so the project's home-grade rule has no grade to search, and grade 6 was searched instead.
g6-2026-042.why: The item gives two rules - 'x: start at 2, add 2' and 'y: start at 4, add 4' - and asks the student to list the first five terms of each pattern and say how corresponding values relate (each y is twice the corresponding x). Nothing in grade 6 asks this. Unit 6 Lessons 16-19 build tables relating two quantities, but those tables come from a context or an equation, never from two 'start at, add' rules, and students are asked to write an equation or interpret a point rather than to generate two patterns and compare corresponding terms. Unit 2's equivalent-ratio tables come closest in shape but are generated by multiplying a ratio, not by repeated addition, and the question asked there is about equivalence, not about a relationship between two generated sequences.
